paragraphs.source_en: My master was lying prone on a white blanket spread out on the veranda, basking in the mild spring sunshine. Sunlight is remarkably fair and impartial: it is just as bright and warm on this shabby house, marked by wild grass growing on its roof, as it is in Mr. Kaneda’s splendid drawing room. Unfortunately, the blanket alone seemed not at all in keeping with the spirit of spring. The manufacturer had woven it as a white blanket, the foreign-goods shop had sold it to its customer as a white blanket, and my master had bought it as a white blanket; but that was twelve or thirteen years ago, and the white blanket had long since ended its white age and was now entering a period of transformation into dark gray. Whether it could pass through that period and enter another in which it turned pitch black remained open to doubt. Even now, having been worn down countless times, its warp and weft can no longer be made out. Therefore to call it a blanket at all is already rather like passing it off under false pretenses. The most accurate name would be to drop the word “wool” and call it simply a rug. My master seems to think that since it has lasted one year, two years, five years, and ten years, it ought to last a lifetime. A remarkably self-indulgent notion. Now, what exactly was he doing, as I have said, lying face down on this historically burdened blanket? He had thrust out both arms to support his chin, and held a cigarette between the fingers of his right hand. He was doing nothing at all; he merely remained like that. Of course, the great truths of the universe may have been spinning incessantly inside that dandruff-covered head of his, but to look at him from the outside, one would never dream of any such thing.
